result: The AGOC vector system uses two spectrally distinguishable fluorescent markers (mOrange and mCherry) embedded in interweaved but incompatible Lox site pairs (LoxP and LoxN). Each marker is flanked upstream by LoxP and downstream by LoxN, creating a configuration where Cre-mediated recombination can excise one marker while leaving the other intact.
evaluation: Claims C3, C19, C26-C29 collectively describe the molecular design of the AGOC vector with appropriate citations for the fluorescent proteins, promoter, and Lox sites. The design is illustrated in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, providing visual confirmation of the vector architecture.

result: The AGOC system enables direct phenotypic identification of all genotypes through Cre-mediated recombination. After recombination, hemizygous individuals carry only one marker and are distinguishable from each other and wild-type. Heterozygotes express both markers, while homozygotes are identified by the lack of one marker.
evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C20-C23 describe the mechanism and phenotypic outcomes of the AGOC system. These are supported by experimental data across all six proof-of-principle lines (Table 1, Figure 3) showing expected Mendelian ratios and successful identification of all genotypes across generations.

result: The AGOC concept was successfully validated in Tribolium castaneum by creating six proof-of-principle transgenic sublines carrying the same transgene at different genomic locations. Single insertions were confirmed, homozygous viability was estimated, and insertion locations were determined for four sublines.
evaluation: Claims C7, C30-C36 describe the initial proof-of-principle experiments. The creation of six independent sublines with documented insertion locations (Supplementary file 3), single insertion confirmation (Supplementary file 1), and viability assessment (Supplementary file 2) provides strong experimental validation.

result: A systematic four-generation mating procedure using a Cre recombinase-expressing helper line successfully created F7 homozygotes for all six AGOC sublines. Progeny scores matched theoretical Mendelian ratios with no significant differences, and all expected phenotypes and genotypes were obtained.
evaluation: Claims C37-C46 describe the mating procedure and its outcomes. Table 1 provides comprehensive data showing observed vs. expected ratios across all generations for all six sublines. Statistical analysis confirmed no significant deviations from Mendelian expectations, and Figure 3 provides phenotypic documentation for sublines #5 and #6.

result: Control experiments with AGOC sublines #5 and #6 confirmed the robustness of the system by successfully conducting the mating procedure with swapped genders and with an alternative Cre recombinase-expressing helper line at a different genomic location.
evaluation: Claims C47-C49 describe control experiments documented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and 2B and Supplementary file 5. These controls demonstrate that the AGOC system functions independently of gender arrangement and helper line genomic location, strengthening the validity of the approach.

result: Five functional AGOC lines with 13 sublines were created for fluorescence live imaging applications. Twelve sublines successfully completed the mating procedure, while one subline (AGOC{ATub'H2B-mEmerald} #4) was heterozygous/homozygous sterile.
evaluation: Claims C50-C54 report the creation and validation of functional imaging lines. The success rate (12/13 sublines) is documented in Supplementary files 6 and 7, with appropriate citations for the promoters and fluorescent tags used. The single failure case is clearly documented.

result: Long-term fluorescence live imaging of embryonic development was successfully performed with three functional homozygous sublines using light-sheet microscopy. The imaged embryos survived, developed to fertile adults, and produced only transgenic progeny when crossed with wild-types, confirming their homozygous status.
evaluation: Claims C55-C59, C118-C119 describe the application of AGOC lines for live imaging. Figure 4 and Videos 1-3 provide visual evidence of successful imaging with distinct expression patterns. The viability and fertility data confirm the homozygous nature of the lines and demonstrate the practical utility of the system.

result: Special cases of transgenesis were successfully handled by the AGOC system, including incomplete recombination in one subline and heterozygous/homozygous lethality in three sublines. Two of the lethal sublines still produced viable homozygotes, while one was sterile at the heterozygous stage.
evaluation: Claims C107-C113 describe experimental observations of special cases documented in the Materials and methods section and supplementary files. The incomplete recombination case (7% in AGOC #4) was handled by continuing with recombined progeny. The lethality cases are documented in Supplementary file 2, with interpretation provided for the observed biased ratios.

result: The AGOC{Zen1'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #2 subline carries the transgene on the X allosome rather than an autosome, requiring a slightly modified mating procedure to obtain F7 homozygous females.
evaluation: Claims C114-C115 describe an X-linked insertion case with the modified procedure illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2. This demonstrates the adaptability of the AGOC system to sex-linked insertions, though it represents a special case requiring procedural modification.

result: A nested insertion case occurred in the AGOC{Zen1'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #3 subline where the transgene inserted into another vector backbone. This was 'corrected' during the AGOC mating procedure when Cre recombinase excised the nested vector sequences.
evaluation: Claims C116-C117 describe a nested insertion confirmed by sequencing (Supplementary file 3). The explanation of how the AGOC system corrects this error through Cre-mediated excision is mechanistically sound and demonstrates an unexpected advantage of the system.

result: The AGOC vector concept avoids temporary ambiguities in genotype determination because all genotypes are directly identifiable by distinct phenotypes, enabling systematic creation of progeny with desired genotypes.
evaluation: Claims C60-C61, C18 describe the key conceptual advantage of the AGOC system. This is supported by the experimental data showing 100% accuracy in phenotypic genotype determination across more than 300 independent instances (C72), with all expected genotypes obtained in all generations (C45).

result: The AGOC approach provides multiple practical advantages over traditional genetic assays: it saves manpower (10 minutes vs. one afternoon for 30-40 individuals), requires no additional consumables, is non-invasive, supports unsynchronized genotyping, simplifies organism handling, and is less error-prone with 100% accuracy across 300+ instances.
evaluation: Claims C62-C72 describe practical advantages supported by time comparisons (C63-C64 with citation), experimental validation (C72), and logical inference from the system design. The 100% accuracy claim is directly supported by the progeny scoring data across all experiments.

result: Compared to balancer chromosome approaches, the AGOC system has advantages despite slightly longer waiting time: balancer lines are only conveniently available for Drosophila, and the AGOC approach works with random/semi-random insertions without requiring knowledge of insertion location.
evaluation: Claims C73-C75 provide a comparison with an alternative method, supported by citation (Ashburner, 1989). The advantages are logical given the demonstrated functionality of AGOC with random insertions (C25, C30) and the documented insertion locations showing diverse genomic positions (C36, Supplementary file 3).

result: The AGOC approach saves resources and simplifies transgenic organism handling by significantly reducing the initial workload required to create homozygous lines and eliminating the need for continuous genotyping during line maintenance.
evaluation: Claims C8, C96-C98 describe resource-saving benefits supported by the demonstrated systematic creation of homozygous lines (C7, C46) and the practical advantages documented in claims C62-C72. The reduction in workload is evident from the time comparison data (C63-C64).

result: The AGOC concept is expected to work in all diploid model organisms including insects, zebrafish, rodents, and plants because it relies on the universal Cre-Lox system. For many insect species, no modification of the basic vector architecture is necessary.
evaluation: Claims C9, C80-C83 make predictions about broader applicability based on the universality of the Cre-Lox system. While the Cre-Lox system is indeed universal (supported by extensive literature), actual functionality in other organisms has not been experimentally demonstrated in this study. The prediction is reasonable but requires validation.

result: The piggyBac transposon system and 3×P3 promoter function properly in multiple insect species and zebrafish. For some species, modifications such as promoter replacement or alternative marker systems are available and documented in the literature.
evaluation: Claims C84-C91 describe the known functionality of system components in various species, supported by extensive citations to the literature. These claims establish the foundation for potential broader applicability of the AGOC system, though they represent prior knowledge rather than new findings.

result: The AGOC concept can potentially be used in knock-out assays to preselect homozygous individuals, reducing the number of animals needed by approximately 75% and contributing to ethical efforts to minimize wasted animals.
evaluation: Claims C10, C93, C101-C102 propose applications in knock-out assays with citations to relevant techniques (CRISPR/Cas9). While the logic is sound based on Mendelian genetics (C100) and the demonstrated functionality of AGOC, this application has not been experimentally validated in the study. The quantitative estimate (75% reduction) is theoretical.

result: The AGOC system can identify and handle special cases of transgenesis, and the distinct phenotypes foster automation potential. Computer-controlled sorting devices with fluorescence detection could be used to sort organisms by genotype.
evaluation: Claims C76-C79 describe advantages regarding special cases (supported by C107-C117) and propose automation applications. While special case handling is demonstrated, the automation potential is speculative with only citations to zebrafish automation systems (C78) as supporting evidence. No automation was actually implemented or tested.

result: A T. castaneum double mutant background strain (PWAS) with completely unpigmented eyes was created and used for the study. The pAVOIAF{#1–#2–#3–#4} vector was designed with minimal-length piggyBac terminal repeats necessary for efficient transposition.
evaluation: Claims C103-C106 describe methodological details supported by citations for the mutations (C103) and terminal repeat length requirements (C106). The creation and use of the PWAS strain is documented in the Materials and methods section, and the vector design is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

result: Diploid transgenic organisms are either hemizygous or homozygous, and traditional transformation markers cannot distinguish between these genotypes, necessitating additional genetic assays that are invasive and resource-intensive.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C14-C17 describe established genetic principles and current limitations of traditional methods. These represent accurate statements of background knowledge in the field, providing context for the AGOC system's advantages. The claims are supported by standard Mendelian genetics and common practice.

result: Mouse, zebrafish, Drosophila melanogaster, and Tribolium castaneum are commonly used model organisms. Transgenesis involves inserting recombinant DNA into the genome, and the piggyBac transposon system allows semi-random genomic insertion.
evaluation: Claims C11-C13, C24-C25 provide background information about model organisms and techniques, supported by appropriate citations. These represent accurate statements of common knowledge and established methods in the field, providing necessary context for the study.

result: Studies using genetically manipulated organisms require maintaining lines for many years with hundreds to thousands of individuals. In knock-out assays with homozygous lethality, lines are maintained as hemizygotes, and crosses produce only 25% homozygous progeny.
evaluation: Claims C92, C94-C95, C99-C100 describe standard practices and Mendelian genetics in transgenic research. These represent accurate statements of common knowledge and established principles, providing context for the practical advantages of the AGOC system.
